setup.zh: 十月十二夜里，你在柴房后面码柴。柴房的门「吱呀」一声开了——马小宝，带着五个人。
setup.en: The night of the twelfth of the tenth month, you're stacking wood behind the woodshed. The woodshed door creaks open — Ma Xiaobao, with five men.

recap.zh: 十月十二夜里，马小宝带五个人堵在柴房后面。你打得过，可你没还手——你数着，二十三下。
recap.en: The night of the twelfth of the tenth month, Ma Xiaobao and five men cornered you behind the woodshed. You could have beaten them; you didn't fight back — you counted: twenty-three.

zh: 十月十二，夜里，柴房后面。
马小宝来了，带着五个人。
en: The twelfth of the tenth month, night, behind the woodshed.
Ma Xiaobao is here, with five men.

text.zh: 刃口是你自己磨的，一刀能劈开一截松木；劈人，你没试过，也不打算今晚试。
text.en: You ground its edge yourself; one blow splits a pine log. You have never tried it on a man and do not mean to start tonight.

text.zh: 木牌凉凉的，一动不动。她睡得正沉。
text.en: The token lies cool and still. She is sound asleep.

story.zh:
十月十二夜里，月亮很好。

这一夜的月亮，后来说书的人讲起来，总要讲得格外好：说那月亮又圆又大，大得像一面铜锣，挂在沉鼎山的山尖上，照得外门后院亮如白昼，照得柴房的瓦片一片一片都镶了银边；说那一夜无风，柴垛上的干草一根都不动，连秋虫都不叫，像是整座山都屏住了气，要看一看这个五行杂灵根的小子，今夜如何过这一关。

其实那一夜的月亮，只是寻常的十二的月亮，还差三天才圆；秋虫也叫的，叫得很吵。说书的人这么讲，是因为这一关实在过得太不像话——一个人蹲在地上挨打，要是连月亮都不给他一个好的，这一段就没法听了。

沈小满蹲在柴房后面，给小狰喂萝卜。这萝卜是伙房大娘给的，大娘自从那回问他拿萝卜干什么、他说练功之后，便认定这孩子练的是一门什么萝卜功，每回见了他，总要往他怀里塞一根，还要叮嘱一句「别练坏了身子」。小狰抱着萝卜，啃得咔嚓咔嚓直响，啃两口，抬头看他一眼，意思是：就这？他便摸摸它那只独角，道：「就这。周师兄说了，外门穷。」

他摸着摸着，手停了下来，压低了声音，对着怀里这一团道：「听着。等会儿要是有人来，你别咬。」

小狰抬起头来看他，嘴里还叼着半截萝卜。

他道：「咬了人，他们就要打你。打你，我就得还手。我还了手，就藏不住了。」想了想，又道，「……实在忍不住，咬一口，就一口。」

小狰把那半截萝卜咽了下去，也不知听懂了没有。

便在这时，身后的柴房门「吱呀」一声开了。

马小宝从柴房里走了出来。他竟是先藏在柴房里的，也不知藏了多久，身上沾着好几根干草，头上顶着一片刨花，手里照旧捏着一块桂花糕。在他身后，一个接一个，又出来了五个人，正是他那五个跟班。六个人在月光底下一字排开，把柴房后面这块巴掌大的空地堵得严严实实。

马小宝把那片刨花从头上拈下来，丢在地上，咬了一口桂花糕，道：「沈小满。听说你收了只畜生？」

小满站起身来，把小狰往身后拨了拨，道：「是狰。」

马小宝道：「我管它是什么。」伸出那只没拿桂花糕的手来，「给我。」

小满道：「它不认生人。」

马小宝道：「它认不认我不管。我认它就行。」冲身后一挥手。

五个人便围了上来。

说时迟那时快，小满脑子里已飞快地过了一遍账。这本账，他这两天夜里在通铺上早算过好几回了，这时候不过是再对一遍：

六个人。五个跟班，都是上一届的老弟子，进门三年，练气三层的两个，练气二层的三个；马小宝练气一层，是三瓶丹药硬喂出来的，底子虚得像一块泡了水的糕。自己呢？练气一层，快摸着第二层的门槛了——只是快，还没摸着。一拳一块青石，他在后山试过的；方才那五个人围上来的脚步，他听得清清楚楚，谁的步子重，谁的步子虚，谁的左脚比右脚慢半拍。

打得过么？

小满想，打得过。未必全打翻，可打得他们一个一个躺在地上哼哼，是打得过的。

可打过了又怎样？

打过了，明天一早，全外门便都知道了：一个五行杂灵根、下下之资、进门才一个月的沈小满，一个人打翻了六个，里头还有两个练气三层的老弟子。周衡会怎么说？褚先生会怎么看？执事会不会来问？观主呢？他一个漏勺，一个月里怎么就能打翻两个练气三层？问下去，便要问到后山那块裂得满是缝的青石，问到他那一夜怎么通的三关，问到他胸口那块木牌，问到木牌里睡着的那一个。

藏。

那一夜银月淡得只剩一双眼睛，一个字一个字地跟他说的，便是这一个字：在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王，不许让任何人知道你在修炼。能装傻就装傻，能示弱就示弱。

他打得过这六个。可他打不过这六个后头的那些。
story.en:
The night of the twelfth of the tenth month, the moon was fine.

That night's moon, when storytellers later told of it, was always made especially fine: round and huge, big as a bronze gong, hung on the peak of Chending Mountain, lighting the back court of the outer court bright as day, rimming every tile of the woodshed roof in silver; no wind that night, not a straw stirring on the woodpile, not even the autumn insects singing, as if the whole mountain held its breath to see how this mixed-root boy would get through the night.

In truth that night's moon was only an ordinary twelfth-day moon, three days short of full, and the autumn insects sang, noisily. The storytellers told it so because the night was got through so unseemly — a boy squatting on the ground being beaten; if not even the moon did right by him, the passage could not be listened to.

Shen Xiaoman was squatting behind the woodshed, feeding Little Zheng a radish. The radish came from the kitchen auntie; ever since she asked what he wanted radishes for and he said "practice," she had decided the boy practised some radish art, and whenever she saw him she pushed one into his coat with a warning — "don't do yourself harm with it." Little Zheng hugged the radish and crunched away, and every two bites looked up at him as if to say: that's it? He stroked its single horn. "That's it. Brother Zhou says the outer court's poor."

Stroking it, his hand stopped, and he lowered his voice to the red bundle in his arms: "Listen. If someone comes in a bit, don't bite."

Little Zheng looked up at him, half a radish still in its mouth.

"Bite someone, and they'll hit you. Hit you, and I'll have to hit back. Hit back, and there's no hiding." He thought, and added, "…If you really can't help it, bite once. Just once."

Little Zheng swallowed the half radish; whether it understood, who knew.

Just then, the woodshed door behind him creaked open.

Ma Xiaobao came out of the woodshed. He had been hiding inside first — who knew how long — and had several straws stuck to him and a wood shaving on his head, and in his hand, as ever, a piece of osmanthus cake. Behind him, one after another, came five more: his five followers. The six stood in a row in the moonlight and blocked that palm-sized patch of ground behind the woodshed tight.

Ma Xiaobao picked the shaving off his head, dropped it, took a bite of cake, and said: "Shen Xiaoman. I hear you've got yourself an animal?"

Xiaoman stood, nudged Little Zheng behind him, and said, "It's a zheng."

"I don't care what it is." Ma Xiaobao held out the hand without the cake. "Give it here."

"It doesn't take to strangers."

"Whether it takes to me I don't care. I take to it — that's enough." He waved a hand behind him.

The five closed in.

Quick as a word, Xiaoman had already run the accounts in his head. He had worked these sums on his bunk several times these two nights; now it was only a matter of checking them once more:

Six men. Five followers, all old disciples from the last intake, three years in — two at the third level of Qi Refining, three at the second; Ma Xiaobao at the first, fed up there by three bottles of pills, his foundation as flimsy as a soaked cake. And himself? The first level, close to the threshold of the second — close, not there. One punch, one boulder: he had tried it on the back mountain. The footsteps of the five closing in, he had heard clearly — whose tread was heavy, whose hollow, whose left foot half a beat behind the right.

Could he beat them?

Xiaoman thought: yes. Not flatten every one, maybe — but leave them lying on the ground groaning one by one: yes.

And after he'd beaten them?

After, by morning the whole outer court would know: Shen Xiaoman, the mixed five-element root, bottom of the bottom, one month in, had flattened six by himself, two of them old disciples at the third level. What would Zhou Heng say? How would Master Chu look at him? Would a steward come asking? And the abbot? A skimmer — how does a skimmer beat two third-level men in a month? Ask further, and they'd ask about the cracked boulder on the back mountain, about how he opened the Three Passes in one night, about the token on his chest, about the one asleep inside it.

Hide.

That night, when Yinyue was so faint only her eyes were left, the word she had said to him, one syllable at a time, was this: until you can beat everyone, let no one know of me; let no one know you cultivate. Play the fool where you can; show weakness where you can.

He could beat these six. He could not beat what stood behind these six.

exits.means: does not fight back, shields the fox token and counts the blows

what.zh: 十月十二，柴房：马小宝等六人，二十三下。利息，另算。
what.en: The twelfth of the tenth month, the woodshed: Ma Xiaobao and five others, twenty-three blows. Interest to be reckoned separately.

story.zh:
小满这一笔账，前前后后，算了不过眨两下眼的工夫。算完了，他把小狰一把捞起来，塞进怀里，拿衣襟裹住，蹲下身去，两只胳膊抱住了头。

拳头和脚，登时像下雨一般落了下来。

后来说书的人说到这一段，总要把醒木一拍，说一句「好一场恶战」。其实这哪里是恶战，恶战要两边打，这一场只一边打，另一边蹲着。可说书的人也有说书的难处：一个人蹲在地上挨了二十三下，这一段若是照实讲，讲不满一炷香，茶钱便收不上来。所以他们讲得很长，长得像是二十三下里，每一下都有一段来历。

照实说，头一下是马小宝踢的。他亲自上前，一脚踢在小满的后背上，踢完了退回去，把桂花糕换到另一只手里，像是这一脚是替桂花糕踢的。

第二下到第五下，是两个练气三层的，一个踢左肩，一个踢右腰，踢得很有章法，一左一右，一右一左，是在外门练了三年的腿法。小满心里数着：二，三，四，五。他一面数，一面想，这两个人的腿法，外门的《基础腿法》第三式，他在讲堂后面的墙上见过图，图上是先抬膝后出脚，这两个人是膝腿同出，少了一个起势——难怪练了三年，还是练气三层。

第六下到第十一下，乱了。五个人一齐上，你一脚我一拳，谁也不让谁，好几回两只脚踢在了一处，踢的人自己先「哎哟」一声。小满缩成一团，护着怀里那只拼命挣扎、「咔咔」直叫的红毛团子，护着胸口那块木牌，把后背、屁股、两条胳膊，一样一样地让出去，只有怀里那一团，让不出去。

第十二下，是马小宝的一记拳头。他挤进人堆里来，一拳砸在小满的左边眼眶上，砸完了自己先甩着手「嘶」了一声。他眼前一黑，跟着一亮，亮起来的时候，左边的天地已经只剩一半了。

第十七下，踢偏了。那一脚本是冲着他腰眼来的，他身子一缩，那一脚擦着他衣裳过去，结结实实踢在了对面一个跟班的小腿迎面骨上。被踢的那一个抱着腿跳了起来，一边跳一边骂，骂的是踢他的那一个，踢他的那一个又骂回去，两个人对骂了三句，才想起地上还蹲着一个，便一齐转过身来，把这三句骂的气，都撒在了第十八下和第十九下上。

小满心想：这两下，冤。

第二十下，有人去扯他怀里的小狰。那只手刚摸到小狰的毛，小狰便一口咬了下去，咬的是虎口，咬得那人「嗷」的一声，甩手就跑，跑出去三丈远，才站住了捂着手嚎。小满趁那工夫，把衣襟裹得更紧了些，心里对怀里那一团道：好样的。别咬了。再咬，就不是二十三下了。

小狰好像听懂了，在他怀里不动了，只是浑身的毛都炸着，一下一下地抖。

第二十一下，第二十二下。

第二十三下，又是马小宝踢的。他走上前来，看了看地上蹲着的这一团，看了看自己那个被狰咬了虎口、还在那边嚎的跟班，脸上的横肉跳了几跳，最后一脚，不轻不重，踢在小满的肩膀上，倒像是给这件事盖了个戳。

踢这一脚的时候，小满正好从胳膊缝里，拿那只还睁得开的右眼，看了马小宝一眼。

后来他常常想起那一眼。他原以为，马小宝踢人的时候，脸上该是得意的，像他爹马三在门框上敲短棍的时候那样，像小时候他捏着桂花糕叫人学狗叫的时候那样。可那一眼看过去，马小宝脸上没有得意。马小宝的脸，在月光底下，是饿的。

像一个吃了一整盒桂花糕、还没吃饱的人。

小满那时候还不懂这是什么意思。他只是记下了。

马小宝喘着粗气，啐了一口。他其实没出什么力，二十三下里他只出了三回手，可他喘得比谁都凶，下巴上那三个黑点，在月光底下亮晶晶的，全是汗。他指着小满怀里那一团，道：「不认主的畜生，我要它何用？留着给你养。」顿了一顿，又道，「下个月初一，公中交两块。」

说罢，带着五个人，扬长而去。那个被咬了虎口的，一面走，一面还回头骂，骂的是狰，不敢骂得太响，怕它听见。

柴房后面，又只剩了一个人和一只狰。

沈小满慢慢地，把抱着头的两只胳膊放下来，身子一歪，仰面躺倒在了泥地里。

泥是凉的，湿的，前两天下过一场雨，柴房后面背阴，一直没干透。他躺在那里，望着天上的月亮。那月亮又圆又亮，照着沉鼎山，照着外门的院墙，照着这一块巴掌大的泥地，也照着泥地里躺着的这一个人，照得很是公平，一点也不偏心。

他嘴里一股血腥味，是咬破了舌头。左边眼睛肿得睁不开，右边眼睛看出去的月亮，也有一点晃。肋骨那儿，一吸气就疼，吸得浅了，疼得轻些；吸得深了，疼得眼前发白。他试了几回，找着了一个不深不浅的口子，便照着那个口子，一口一口地喘。

他对着月亮，很轻地骂了一声：「……你爷爷的。」

骂完了，想起来，又补了一句：「……爷爷，不是说你。」

小狰从他怀里钻了出来，抖了抖一身炸开的毛，爬到他胸口上，低下头，拿它那只独角，一下一下，轻轻地顶他的脸。那角是硬的，顶在他肿起来的眼眶上，疼。他没躲。

他咧了咧嘴，一咧便疼，道：「……没事。」又道，「账，记着呢。」

一下，两下，十下，二十下，二十三下。他在心里又数了一遍，一下都不少。
story.en:
Xiaoman's whole reckoning took no longer than two blinks. When it was done, he scooped up Little Zheng, stuffed it in his coat, wrapped his lapel round it, squatted down, and wrapped both arms round his head.

Fists and feet came down at once like rain.

In later years, when storytellers reached this passage, they always smacked the gavel and said, "What a desperate fight!" It was no fight at all: a fight takes two sides, and here one side hit and the other squatted. But storytellers have their troubles too: a boy squatting on the ground taking twenty-three blows, told as it was, would not fill a stick of incense, and the tea money would never be collected. So they told it long — long enough that each of the twenty-three seemed to have a history of its own.

To tell it truly: the first was Ma Xiaobao's. He stepped up himself, kicked Xiaoman in the back, stepped back, and shifted his osmanthus cake to the other hand, as if the kick had been on the cake's behalf.

The second to the fifth were the two at the third level, one kicking the left shoulder, one the right side, very methodically — left, right, right, left — the leg form they had practised three years in the outer court. Xiaoman counted in his head: two, three, four, five. As he counted he thought: the outer court's *Basic Leg Forms*, third stance — he had seen the chart on the wall behind the lecture hall: knee first, then foot. These two threw knee and foot together and missed the lift — no wonder, three years in and still at the third level.

From the sixth to the eleventh it fell apart. The five piled in at once, a foot from you, a fist from me, nobody giving way, and more than once two feet met each other, the kickers yelping first. Xiaoman curled into a ball, shielding the frantic, chittering red bundle in his coat, shielding the token on his chest; his back, his rump, both arms he gave up one by one; only the bundle in his coat he could not give up.

The twelfth was Ma Xiaobao's fist. He squeezed into the crowd and brought it down on Xiaoman's left eye socket, then shook his own hand and hissed. Xiaoman's sight went black, then bright, and when it came back, the left half of the world was gone.

The seventeenth went wide. It was aimed at the small of his back; he tucked in, it grazed his clothes and landed square on the shin of a follower across from him. The kicked one hopped about swearing at the kicker, the kicker swore back, three rounds of it, before they remembered the one squatting on the ground and turned together and put all three rounds of temper into the eighteenth and nineteenth.

Xiaoman thought: those two were unjust.

At the twentieth, someone reached for the zheng in his coat. The hand had barely touched its fur when Little Zheng bit — the web of the thumb — so hard the man howled, snatched his hand back and ran, and only stopped three rods off, clutching it and wailing. Xiaoman used the moment to wrap his coat tighter, and told the bundle in his heart: good. No more. Bite again, and it won't be twenty-three.

Little Zheng seemed to understand; it lay still in his coat, only every hair on end, shivering.

The twenty-first. The twenty-second.

The twenty-third was Ma Xiaobao's again. He came forward, looked at the huddle on the ground, looked at his own follower, the one bitten on the thumb and still howling over there, his face twitching, and the last kick, neither light nor hard, landed on Xiaoman's shoulder — as though stamping a seal on the whole affair.

As that kick came, Xiaoman happened to look at Ma Xiaobao, through a gap between his arms, with the one eye that would still open.

He often thought of that look afterwards. He had supposed that Ma Xiaobao, kicking a man, would look pleased — the way Ma San looked rapping his cudgel on a door frame, the way Xiaobao looked when he was little, holding up osmanthus cake and telling someone to bark like a dog. But when he looked, there was no pleasure on Ma Xiaobao's face. Ma Xiaobao's face, in the moonlight, was hungry.

Like a man who has eaten a whole box of osmanthus cake and is still not full.

Xiaoman did not yet understand what that meant. He only noted it.

Ma Xiaobao was panting hard, and spat. He had hardly exerted himself — three of the twenty-three were his — but he panted worse than any of them, and the three black specks on his chin glistened with sweat in the moonlight. He pointed at the bundle in Xiaoman's coat: "A beast that won't know its master — what use is it to me? Keep it and feed it yourself." Then, after a pause: "The first of next month, the common fund is two."

And with that he swaggered off with his five. The one bitten on the thumb kept looking back and swearing as he went — swearing at the zheng, but not too loud, in case it heard.

Behind the woodshed there was once again only one boy and one zheng.

Shen Xiaoman slowly lowered the arms wrapped round his head, tipped over, and lay flat on his back in the mud.

The mud was cold and wet; it had rained two days before, and behind the woodshed, in the shade, it had never quite dried. He lay there looking up at the moon. The moon was round and bright; it shone on Chending Mountain, on the wall of the outer court, on this palm's-breadth of mud, on the boy lying in it — very fair, favouring no one.

His mouth tasted of blood; he had bitten his tongue. The left eye was swollen shut; through the right, the moon wobbled a little. At his ribs, every breath hurt — shallow, less; deep, so much his sight went white. He tried a few times, found a breath neither deep nor shallow, and breathed by it, one mouthful at a time.

To the moon, very softly, he swore: "…Your grandfather's."

Having sworn, he remembered, and added: "…Grandpa, not you."

Little Zheng wriggled out of his coat, shook out its bristling fur, climbed onto his chest, bent its head, and with its single horn nudged his face, gently, again and again. The horn was hard, and pressed against his swollen eye, it hurt. He didn't pull away.

He grinned — it hurt to grin — and said, "…I'm all right." And: "It's in the books."

One, two, ten, twenty, twenty-three. He counted them over again in his head; not one short.

exits.means: clenches the fists, nearly fights back

what.zh: 十月十二，柴房：马小宝等六人，二十三下。利息，另算。
what.en: The twelfth of the tenth month, the woodshed: Ma Xiaobao and five others, twenty-three blows. Interest to be reckoned separately.

story.zh:
他攥紧了拳头。后山那块青石上的缝，从上到下，一拳，就一拳。

他想起那一夜，木牌里那个淡得只剩一双眼睛的声音，一个字一个字说的那个字。

他松开了拳头，把小狰一把捞起来，塞进怀里，拿衣襟裹住，蹲下身去，两只胳膊抱住了头。

拳头和脚，登时像下雨一般落了下来。

后来说书的人说到这一段，总要把醒木一拍，说一句「好一场恶战」。其实这哪里是恶战，恶战要两边打，这一场只一边打，另一边蹲着。可说书的人也有说书的难处：一个人蹲在地上挨了二十三下，这一段若是照实讲，讲不满一炷香，茶钱便收不上来。所以他们讲得很长，长得像是二十三下里，每一下都有一段来历。

照实说，头一下是马小宝踢的。他亲自上前，一脚踢在小满的后背上，踢完了退回去，把桂花糕换到另一只手里，像是这一脚是替桂花糕踢的。

第二下到第五下，是两个练气三层的，一个踢左肩，一个踢右腰，踢得很有章法，一左一右，一右一左，是在外门练了三年的腿法。小满心里数着：二，三，四，五。他一面数，一面想，这两个人的腿法，外门的《基础腿法》第三式，他在讲堂后面的墙上见过图，图上是先抬膝后出脚，这两个人是膝腿同出，少了一个起势——难怪练了三年，还是练气三层。

第六下到第十一下，乱了。五个人一齐上，你一脚我一拳，谁也不让谁，好几回两只脚踢在了一处，踢的人自己先「哎哟」一声。小满缩成一团，护着怀里那只拼命挣扎、「咔咔」直叫的红毛团子，护着胸口那块木牌，把后背、屁股、两条胳膊，一样一样地让出去，只有怀里那一团，让不出去。

第十二下，是马小宝的一记拳头。他挤进人堆里来，一拳砸在小满的左边眼眶上，砸完了自己先甩着手「嘶」了一声。他眼前一黑，跟着一亮，亮起来的时候，左边的天地已经只剩一半了。

第十七下，踢偏了。那一脚本是冲着他腰眼来的，他身子一缩，那一脚擦着他衣裳过去，结结实实踢在了对面一个跟班的小腿迎面骨上。被踢的那一个抱着腿跳了起来，一边跳一边骂，骂的是踢他的那一个，踢他的那一个又骂回去，两个人对骂了三句，才想起地上还蹲着一个，便一齐转过身来，把这三句骂的气，都撒在了第十八下和第十九下上。

小满心想：这两下，冤。

第二十下，有人去扯他怀里的小狰。那只手刚摸到小狰的毛，小狰便一口咬了下去，咬的是虎口，咬得那人「嗷」的一声，甩手就跑，跑出去三丈远，才站住了捂着手嚎。小满趁那工夫，把衣襟裹得更紧了些，心里对怀里那一团道：好样的。别咬了。再咬，就不是二十三下了。

小狰好像听懂了，在他怀里不动了，只是浑身的毛都炸着，一下一下地抖。

第二十一下，第二十二下。

第二十三下，又是马小宝踢的。他走上前来，看了看地上蹲着的这一团，看了看自己那个被狰咬了虎口、还在那边嚎的跟班，脸上的横肉跳了几跳，最后一脚，不轻不重，踢在小满的肩膀上，倒像是给这件事盖了个戳。

踢这一脚的时候，小满正好从胳膊缝里，拿那只还睁得开的右眼，看了马小宝一眼。

后来他常常想起那一眼。他原以为，马小宝踢人的时候，脸上该是得意的，像他爹马三在门框上敲短棍的时候那样，像小时候他捏着桂花糕叫人学狗叫的时候那样。可那一眼看过去，马小宝脸上没有得意。马小宝的脸，在月光底下，是饿的。

像一个吃了一整盒桂花糕、还没吃饱的人。

小满那时候还不懂这是什么意思。他只是记下了。

马小宝喘着粗气，啐了一口。他其实没出什么力，二十三下里他只出了三回手，可他喘得比谁都凶，下巴上那三个黑点，在月光底下亮晶晶的，全是汗。他指着小满怀里那一团，道：「不认主的畜生，我要它何用？留着给你养。」顿了一顿，又道，「下个月初一，公中交两块。」

说罢，带着五个人，扬长而去。那个被咬了虎口的，一面走，一面还回头骂，骂的是狰，不敢骂得太响，怕它听见。

柴房后面，又只剩了一个人和一只狰。

沈小满慢慢地，把抱着头的两只胳膊放下来，身子一歪，仰面躺倒在了泥地里。

泥是凉的，湿的，前两天下过一场雨，柴房后面背阴，一直没干透。他躺在那里，望着天上的月亮。那月亮又圆又亮，照着沉鼎山，照着外门的院墙，照着这一块巴掌大的泥地，也照着泥地里躺着的这一个人，照得很是公平，一点也不偏心。

他嘴里一股血腥味，是咬破了舌头。左边眼睛肿得睁不开，右边眼睛看出去的月亮，也有一点晃。肋骨那儿，一吸气就疼，吸得浅了，疼得轻些；吸得深了，疼得眼前发白。他试了几回，找着了一个不深不浅的口子，便照着那个口子，一口一口地喘。

他对着月亮，很轻地骂了一声：「……你爷爷的。」

骂完了，想起来，又补了一句：「……爷爷，不是说你。」

小狰从他怀里钻了出来，抖了抖一身炸开的毛，爬到他胸口上，低下头，拿它那只独角，一下一下，轻轻地顶他的脸。那角是硬的，顶在他肿起来的眼眶上，疼。他没躲。

他咧了咧嘴，一咧便疼，道：「……没事。」又道，「账，记着呢。」

一下，两下，十下，二十下，二十三下。他在心里又数了一遍，一下都不少。
story.en:
He clenched his fists. The seam in the boulder on the back mountain, top to bottom. One punch. Just one.

He thought of that night, and the voice in the token, so faint only a pair of eyes was left, saying that one word, one syllable at a time.

He unclenched his fists, scooped up Little Zheng, stuffed it in his coat, wrapped his lapel round it, squatted down, and wrapped both arms round his head.

Fists and feet came down at once like rain.

In later years, when storytellers reached this passage, they always smacked the gavel and said, "What a desperate fight!" It was no fight at all: a fight takes two sides, and here one side hit and the other squatted. But storytellers have their troubles too: a boy squatting on the ground taking twenty-three blows, told as it was, would not fill a stick of incense, and the tea money would never be collected. So they told it long — long enough that each of the twenty-three seemed to have a history of its own.

To tell it truly: the first was Ma Xiaobao's. He stepped up himself, kicked Xiaoman in the back, stepped back, and shifted his osmanthus cake to the other hand, as if the kick had been on the cake's behalf.

The second to the fifth were the two at the third level, one kicking the left shoulder, one the right side, very methodically — left, right, right, left — the leg form they had practised three years in the outer court. Xiaoman counted in his head: two, three, four, five. As he counted he thought: the outer court's *Basic Leg Forms*, third stance — he had seen the chart on the wall behind the lecture hall: knee first, then foot. These two threw knee and foot together and missed the lift — no wonder, three years in and still at the third level.

From the sixth to the eleventh it fell apart. The five piled in at once, a foot from you, a fist from me, nobody giving way, and more than once two feet met each other, the kickers yelping first. Xiaoman curled into a ball, shielding the frantic, chittering red bundle in his coat, shielding the token on his chest; his back, his rump, both arms he gave up one by one; only the bundle in his coat he could not give up.

The twelfth was Ma Xiaobao's fist. He squeezed into the crowd and brought it down on Xiaoman's left eye socket, then shook his own hand and hissed. Xiaoman's sight went black, then bright, and when it came back, the left half of the world was gone.

The seventeenth went wide. It was aimed at the small of his back; he tucked in, it grazed his clothes and landed square on the shin of a follower across from him. The kicked one hopped about swearing at the kicker, the kicker swore back, three rounds of it, before they remembered the one squatting on the ground and turned together and put all three rounds of temper into the eighteenth and nineteenth.

Xiaoman thought: those two were unjust.

At the twentieth, someone reached for the zheng in his coat. The hand had barely touched its fur when Little Zheng bit — the web of the thumb — so hard the man howled, snatched his hand back and ran, and only stopped three rods off, clutching it and wailing. Xiaoman used the moment to wrap his coat tighter, and told the bundle in his heart: good. No more. Bite again, and it won't be twenty-three.

Little Zheng seemed to understand; it lay still in his coat, only every hair on end, shivering.

The twenty-first. The twenty-second.

The twenty-third was Ma Xiaobao's again. He came forward, looked at the huddle on the ground, looked at his own follower, the one bitten on the thumb and still howling over there, his face twitching, and the last kick, neither light nor hard, landed on Xiaoman's shoulder — as though stamping a seal on the whole affair.

As that kick came, Xiaoman happened to look at Ma Xiaobao, through a gap between his arms, with the one eye that would still open.

He often thought of that look afterwards. He had supposed that Ma Xiaobao, kicking a man, would look pleased — the way Ma San looked rapping his cudgel on a door frame, the way Xiaobao looked when he was little, holding up osmanthus cake and telling someone to bark like a dog. But when he looked, there was no pleasure on Ma Xiaobao's face. Ma Xiaobao's face, in the moonlight, was hungry.

Like a man who has eaten a whole box of osmanthus cake and is still not full.

Xiaoman did not yet understand what that meant. He only noted it.

Ma Xiaobao was panting hard, and spat. He had hardly exerted himself — three of the twenty-three were his — but he panted worse than any of them, and the three black specks on his chin glistened with sweat in the moonlight. He pointed at the bundle in Xiaoman's coat: "A beast that won't know its master — what use is it to me? Keep it and feed it yourself." Then, after a pause: "The first of next month, the common fund is two."

And with that he swaggered off with his five. The one bitten on the thumb kept looking back and swearing as he went — swearing at the zheng, but not too loud, in case it heard.

Behind the woodshed there was once again only one boy and one zheng.

Shen Xiaoman slowly lowered the arms wrapped round his head, tipped over, and lay flat on his back in the mud.

The mud was cold and wet; it had rained two days before, and behind the woodshed, in the shade, it had never quite dried. He lay there looking up at the moon. The moon was round and bright; it shone on Chending Mountain, on the wall of the outer court, on this palm's-breadth of mud, on the boy lying in it — very fair, favouring no one.

His mouth tasted of blood; he had bitten his tongue. The left eye was swollen shut; through the right, the moon wobbled a little. At his ribs, every breath hurt — shallow, less; deep, so much his sight went white. He tried a few times, found a breath neither deep nor shallow, and breathed by it, one mouthful at a time.

To the moon, very softly, he swore: "…Your grandfather's."

Having sworn, he remembered, and added: "…Grandpa, not you."

Little Zheng wriggled out of his coat, shook out its bristling fur, climbed onto his chest, bent its head, and with its single horn nudged his face, gently, again and again. The horn was hard, and pressed against his swollen eye, it hurt. He didn't pull away.

He grinned — it hurt to grin — and said, "…I'm all right." And: "It's in the books."

One, two, ten, twenty, twenty-three. He counted them over again in his head; not one short.
